deep.reconstruction:
This folio contains no mathematical derivations. It is a sequence of philosophical aphorisms from Hilbert's notebook (Notizbuch), continuing the themes of the previous page: pre-established harmony between thought and being, monism, and the axiomatic method as the universal form of thought.

(1) Every science feeds mathematics. Physicists, philosophers, psychologists and biologists, insofar as they produce something lasting, are said to be ultimately only gathering material for mathematics.

(2) Einstein to Sommerfeld. As support, Hilbert quotes from memory or from a copy Einstein's letter to Sommerfeld of 29 Oct 1912. In it Einstein says he is now working exclusively on gravitation theory. He has never in his life toiled so hard. He has gained great respect for mathematics, whose subtler parts he had until then regarded as pure luxury. Hilbert marks omissions with dashes.

(3) A physical grounding of logic. Hilbert proposes trying to ground logic itself by physical-mechanical considerations: thinking triggers mechanical contacts ('Berührungen'). Otherwise, he notes, pre-established harmony would be impossible. He asks whether microbes think. He states that 'thinking correctly' means thinking so that the experiment agrees.

(4) Why logical conclusions come true. He asks why whatever is logically concluded from true premises must actually happen. His answer: logic is itself nothing but a 'happening' (Geschehen), one that is independent of time and place, i.e. invariant. Our thinking rests on the existence of such invariants. This is an invariance-theoretic reading of logic, plainly influenced by relativity and invariant theory.

(5) The 'Ω-thesis' (begins at the bottom of the page, continues overleaf). One can apply the laws of probability to logic and to mathematical assertions with the same right and success as to empirical facts. The previous page gives the examples: the statistical principle of averaging, the irrationality of √2, and 1s and 2s occurring asymptotically equally often in the decimal expansion of π.

There is nothing to reconstruct in formulas. The only implicit mathematical content is the heuristic that the digits of π are equidistributed, and more generally that probabilistic reasoning applies to deterministic mathematical statements.
errors: No mathematical errors, since there is no computation.

The Einstein quotation is somewhat paraphrased and abridged (indicated by Hilbert's dashes). To my recollection, Einstein's original reads 'mit dem Gravitationsproblem', not 'mit Gravitationstheorie'. It also contains 'in meiner Einfalt' before 'für puren Luxus' and a mention of help from a Zurich mathematician friend (Grossmann); these are omitted here. Treat this as recalled, not checked against the edition.

The claim that logic must be grounded via mechanical brain contacts, and that 'richtig denken' means agreement with experiment, is a philosophical conjecture, not a justified step. It is also in tension with Hilbert's later formalist and finitist position.

results.what: Thesis that all lasting science ultimately supplies material for mathematics; supported by Einstein's 1912 letter to Sommerfeld on his new respect for mathematics.
results.modern_name: Hilbert's view of the axiomatization and mathematization of the sciences (cf. 6th problem, 'Axiomatisches Denken' 1917)
results.usually_credited_to: Hilbert (published views 1900, 1917, 1930 Königsberg address); the letter is Einstein to Sommerfeld, 29 Oct 1912

results.what: Logic as an invariant 'Geschehen', independent of time and place; the existence of invariants is the basis of thought; physical-mechanical grounding of logic.
results.modern_name: Naturalized / physicalist epistemology of logic; invariance conception of logic (cf. later Tarski 1966 'What are logical notions?')
results.usually_credited_to: Diverse (Mach, Boltzmann-style evolutionary epistemology; invariance view of logicality: Klein-program analogies, Tarski 1966)

results.what: 'Ω-thesis': probability laws may be applied to mathematical statements as to empirical facts (e.g. equal asymptotic frequency of digits of π).
results.modern_name: Probabilistic heuristics in number theory / normality of π (Borel 1909); Cramér model; Pólya's plausible reasoning
results.usually_credited_to: Borel (normal numbers, 1909); Hardy–Littlewood (1923) and Cramér (1936) for probabilistic prime heuristics; Pólya (1954) for plausible reasoning

deep.surprise_reason: The page is philosophical commentary of the kind known from Hilbert's notebooks, already studied by Corry, Sauer, Majer and others. Hilbert copying Einstein's 1912 letter to Sommerfeld is a nice documentary detail on the Göttingen–Munich exchange around relativity, but the letter itself is published. The 'Ω-thesis' (probabilistic reasoning about mathematical truths) is an interesting early statement, but no theorem or method is given.

checkable.asserts: Empirical check of the heuristic invoked by the Ω-thesis: in the first 20000 decimals of π, digits 1 and 2 occur with nearly equal frequency.
√2 is irrational (example named on the previous page as a mathematical fact to which statistical reasoning was compared).

transcription_corrections: Line 1: 'sondern die alle' is more likely 'sondern sie alle' in the image.
'Denken die Mi[?]kroben?' should read 'Denken die Mikroben?' (hyphenated 'Mi-/kroben', written somewhat illegibly).
'was [-nicht-] logisch richtig' is correct: 'nicht' is struck through.
In 'von Zeit u. [-Ra-] Ort', the struck fragment is plausibly the start of 'Raum'.
'Eine Art Ω-These' is confirmed; the symbol is a capital Omega.
